common_name: Prolifica Autumn Fern (Proliferous Japanese Shield Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this selection roots small plantlets along mature fronds that can be detached and potted up as an easy way to increase the clone.

directions: This selection of the popular autumn fern shares the species' coppery-pink new growth maturing to glossy deep green, but it also forms small plantlets along the rachis of older fronds, an unusual proliferous habit for a Dryopteris. Gardeners can peg a frond to moist soil or simply pot up rooted plantlets as they form, giving an easy way to multiply the clone without disturbing the parent crown. Like the species it is evergreen to semi-evergreen in milder winters and prefers consistently moist, humus-rich soil in open to full shade. Groom out tattered old fronds in late winter before the pink-flushed fiddleheads unfurl.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade with some morning light to bring out the best frond color; a twisted-frond sport of the species, propagated by division to remain true to type.

directions: This sport of the Japanese painted fern arose as a twisted-frond mutation and keeps the species' silvery-gray pinnae overlaid with wine-red midribs, but each frond spirals and twists along its length instead of lying flat, giving the clump a restless, textured movement unlike any other painted fern selection. It forms a slowly spreading, deciduous clump similar in scale to the species and colors best with a little morning sun and consistently moist, humus-rich soil. New fiddleheads emerge deep burgundy in spring, and the twisting habit becomes more pronounced as fronds mature through the season. Divide congested crowns in early spring to maintain vigor and to propagate the twisted form true to type.

planting.note: Plant divisions in sharply drained, humus-poor soil or in rock crevices and old walls in partial shade to partial sun; mimics the lime-rich wall and ledge habitats where this historic selection was first found.

directions: Found growing wild on an old wall in southwest England in the seventeenth century and named for the man credited with discovering it, this is among the oldest fern cultivars still in cultivation, predating the Victorian fern-collecting craze by two centuries. Its evergreen fronds are more finely and deeply divided than the wild Welsh polypody, with narrow, somewhat congested pinnae that give the plant a softer, more feathery texture overall. Like the species it grows naturally on rock ledges, old mortared walls, and tree bark rather than ordinary garden soil, so it performs best in sharply drained, lean conditions and tolerates drier, shadier sites than most garden ferns. New fronds emerge in autumn and persist through winter before the plant rests through the heat of summer.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in partial to full shade; performs poorly in strongly acidic ground, so add lime or crushed limestone grit where native soil is acidic.

directions: One of the long-cultivated historic forms of hart's tongue fern, this selection carries the same undivided, strap-shaped, glossy evergreen fronds as the species, but each frond margin ripples in a regular, gentle wave rather than lying flat, a subtler effect than the heavily ruffled 'Crispum'. It forms the same dense, upright rosette as the species and shares its preference for neutral to alkaline, humus-rich soil, often thriving at the base of limestone or old mortared walls where lime leaches into the ground. Fronds persist through winter and should be groomed of tattered growth in early spring just before new fronds unfurl from the crown. Divide congested, multi-crowned clumps only occasionally, since hart's tongue fern resents frequent disturbance.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in partial to full shade; avoid cutting back fronds except to remove winter damage, since the crests are the main ornamental feature.

directions: This historic hart's tongue fern selection keeps the species' smooth, undivided, strap-shaped evergreen frond, but each frond terminates in a broad, flattened, fan-like crest instead of tapering to a point, an effect that is most pronounced on vigorous, well-grown plants. Like the species it prefers neutral to alkaline, humus-rich soil and struggles in strongly acidic ground, often thriving near the lime-leaching base of a masonry wall or path edge. Fronds are evergreen and should only be groomed of winter-damaged growth in early spring, since removing fronds prematurely sacrifices a full season of the crested display. It increases slowly from the crown and is best left undisturbed for several years between divisions.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mulch over winter in the colder part of its hardiness range.

directions: This variegated selection of the East Indian holly fern, native to East Asia, carries a pale yellow-green stripe down the center of each glossy, leathery pinna set against darker green blade tissue, a patterning that holds up well even in fairly deep shade where many variegated plants fade. Its broadly triangular, twice-cut fronds arise from a slowly creeping rhizome and stay evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild winters, giving the shade garden structure through the colder months. It prefers humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil and appreciates a protective winter mulch toward the cold end of its range. Groom out tattered fronds in late winter before new croziers emerge, and divide the spreading rhizome in spring only when clumps become crowded.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; a Pacific Northwest native of moist conifer forests, it browns quickly if the soil dries out.

directions: Western oak fern forms a low, spreading carpet of delicate, broadly triangular, thrice-cut fronds carried singly along a slender creeping rhizome rather than arising in a tight clump, giving it a lacy, groundcover-like presence under conifers and bigleaf maples across its native range from Alaska south through the Pacific Northwest. It closely resembles and is sometimes confused with the more widespread Gymnocarpium dryopteris, but tends toward finer division and a more southerly, coastal distribution. Its thin-textured deciduous fronds emerge in spring and brown quickly if the soil dries out, so it needs consistently moist, humus-rich soil and cool, deep shade to perform well. It spreads gradually into an attractive patch and works best as a small-scale groundcover beneath larger ferns and woodland perennials rather than as a specimen plant.

planting.note: Plant divisions in gritty, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; well suited to crevices in a shaded rock garden or retaining wall where drainage is sharp.

directions: Unlike the finely cut, lacy fronds typical of most Woodsia species, this East Asian species produces once-cut, pinnately divided fronds with broad, toothed pinnae that give it a coarser, holly-like texture, the source of its common name. It forms a dense, low tuft from a short rhizome and is naturally found on rocky slopes, cliff crevices, and stony banks in Japan, Korea, and China, making it well suited to a shaded rock garden or the crevices of a retaining wall where drainage is sharp. Fronds are deciduous to semi-evergreen depending on climate, emerging in spring and persisting into early winter in milder gardens. It tolerates drier soil than many woodland ferns once established but still appreciates consistent moisture at the root zone through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, ideally near a seepage area or on a shaded slope that mimics its native streambank and rocky-seep habitat.

directions: This compact selection of western maidenhair fern was chosen for pinnae that overlap more tightly along the frond than the open, airy arrangement typical of the species, giving a denser, more congested fan-shaped frond held on the same wiry, blackish stems. It shares the species' native preference for cool, moist rock seeps and streambanks across western North America, though garden plants adapt well to ordinary woodland soil with regular watering. Fronds emerge with a pinkish-bronze flush in spring before maturing to blue-green, dying back with hard frost in colder zones but persisting nearly evergreen in milder coastal gardens. Its smaller, denser habit suits a shaded rock garden or container planting better than the more spreading species form.

planting.note: Move divisions or container plants outdoors to a shaded spot after all danger of frost has passed; grow as a houseplant or bring under cover for winter outside zones 9-11.

directions: A golden-yellow sport of the classic Boston fern, this selection produces the same gracefully arching, finely divided fronds from a spreading rhizome, but new growth emerges a bright chartreuse-gold that settles to yellow-green as fronds mature, instead of the plain deep green of the species. It shares the Boston fern's vigor and quickly fills a hanging basket or shaded bed with cascading fronds in a single warm, humid growing season. Outdoors it survives as a perennial only in frost-free or nearly frost-free gardens and is best grown as a container or porch specimen elsewhere, brought indoors well before the first frost. It needs consistently moist soil and high humidity, browning at the frond tips quickly if it dries out or sits in dry indoor heat.

planting.note: Move container plants outdoors to a sheltered, deeply shaded spot after all danger of frost has passed; grow as a conservatory or large container plant outside zones 9-11.

directions: This robust tropical Asian relative of the lady ferns produces large, twice-cut, broadly triangular fronds from a stout, upright rhizome, eventually building a short trunk-like base reminiscent of a small tree fern on long-established plants. Its common name refers to the small plantlets that form along the rachis and pinnae of mature fronds, which root readily where they touch moist soil or can be detached and potted up to propagate the plant without disturbing the parent. It needs constant warmth, high humidity, and evenly moist, humus-rich soil to perform well, and will not tolerate frost or prolonged dry spells. In frost-free gardens it makes a bold textural specimen for a sheltered, shaded border; elsewhere it is best grown as a large container or conservatory plant.
